Wind gusts were estimated around 60 mph with a thunderstorm outflow.
Numerous trees were damaged and power lines were blown down in the city of Peoria.
Several trees were toppled, one of which fell onto power lines and caused a power outage in a subdivision near the Greater Peoria Airport.
Several trees were blown down between East Peoria and Creve Coeur on Pekin Avenue.
A one foot diameter tree fell onto a house in Creve Coeur.
Several trees were blown down on cars and houses in the 1100 block of Springfield Road in East Peoria. Wind damage occurred over a 2 block radius.

A funnel cloud was sighted by numerous people between Hudson and Lexington, including the Lake Bloomington recreational areas. There was no evidence of debris near the ground, and no reports of damage.
Spotters reported a funnel cloud near the town of Henning. The funnel was short lived and there were no reports of debris or damage.
A large shed was blown apart by damaging winds from an isolated thunderstorm. Debris was blown into nearby trees and power lines.
Storm spotters reported penny sized hail near Metamora.
Spotters reported nickel sized hail just west of Washington.
Spotters reported penny sized hail near Eureka.
Hail up to 2.00 inches in diameter damaged several vehicles southeast of the town of Auburn.
The hail did significant crop damage to a bean field near the town of Pisgah.
Hail ranged from pea sized to half-dollar sized.
Large hail which increased in size from 1.00 in diameter to 2.50 in diameter damaged roofs and numerous cars in Mount Pulaski. A soybean field just southwest of the city was also destroyed.
Hail up to 1.50 inches in diameter damaged four cars, and did shingle damage to several houses.

A microburst, with wind speeds estimated at 80 mph, flattened about 100 acres of corn in southern Champaign County about 4.5 miles east-southeast of Philo. Most of the corn will be able to be harvested, with about 15% destroyed.
A lightning strike destroyed a tree, and killed a Chinese Sharpei dog which was chained to the tree.
An auto body shop in the town of Fisher was struck by lightning, which ignited a fire. The building sustained minor damage. There was one person in the building, but they escaped without injury.
Wind gust estimated by coop observer. Only minor damage to tree limbs.
Measured wind gust of 60 mph with downed tree limbs and pea sized hail.
Significant weather observer estimated a 50 knot wind gust with minor damage to small tree limbs.
Power lines were blown down, power poles were snapped, there was extensive damage to trees, and some house roof damage was reported due to falling trees in the Lake Camelot subdivision.
Large tree limbs were blown down at Spoon River College, and some corn fields were flattened southwest of Canton.
Large tree branches and small trees were blown down.
Large tree branches were blown down near Abingdon.
Significant weather observer reported golf ball sized hail north of Abingdon.
A tree was blown down into powerlines, causing a fire and power outages to parts of Decatur.
The roof of a covered bridge was blown off at the C.H. Moore Homestead in Clinton.
A large restaurant sign was blown over on the west side of Rantoul.
The ground was covered with hailstones.  Some minor damage to vehicles and buildings was reported.
Numerous trees were blown down about 2 miles northeast of Mahomet.  A tree was snapped off and fell onto a deck.  Metal roofing was peeled off a horse barn.
A large tree was blown down onto power lines...taking down a half mile stretch of lines.
Numerous 4-inch diameter tree limbs were blown down in Russellville.
A portion of the canvas roof over the Multi-Purpose Arena at the Illinois State Fairgrounds in Springfield was damaged by strong winds.
A grain bin was blown over, then tumbled for 1.5 miles near Ashmore.

Icy conditions caused a driver to lose control of his car and crash into an oncoming sport utility vehicle on Illinois Route 1 about a mile north of I-70 in Clark County.  The driver of the car was killed, while the driver of the SUV was transported to the hospital.

Numerous accidents were reported across Bloomington-Normal due to icy road conditions.  The most serious accident resulted in 5 injuries as two cars collided at Euclid and Oakland Avenues in Bloomington.

Three to five inches of snow fell across Tazewell County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.  In addition, a 62 year-old man died of cardiac arrest at his home in Morton on January 13th after shoveling the snow.

Three to five inches of snow fell across Fulton County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.  One man was killed when his pickup truck slid off County Road 2 near Ellisville during the morning of January 12th.  At least two other people were injured in other traffic accidents across the county.

Three to five inches of snow fell across Marshall County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.  One man was killed when his car collided with an oncoming semi truck on Illinois Route 17 near Sparland during the morning of January 12th.
Three to five inches of snow fell across McLean County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.
Two to three inches of snow fell across Macon County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.
Two to three inches of snow fell across Sangamon County, resulting in numerous traffic accidents.
Several trees were damaged, including one that fell onto a car.  In addition, minor siding damage was reported and a swing set was blown into a field.
Numerous trees were blown down in Mt. Auburn.
Numerous tree limbs were blown down and a shed was damaged in Assumption.
A tree was blown down onto Route 130 west of Hugo blocking one lane of traffic.
A large tree was blown down onto Vermilion Street in Danville.
A tractor trailer was blown over on Interstate 72 at mile marker 134 near Warrensburg.
A piece of aluminum roof framing was torn from the front of a detached garage in Oakley.
A tree was blown onto a house in Champaign, causing roof and wall damage.
A traffic light was knocked down in Pana.
Lightning struck a barn northwest of Mechanicsburg causing a fire.
Lightning struck a power pole, knocking down power lines across a road in Danville.
Numerous trees were blown down about 2 miles southeast of Xenia.
A large pine tree was uprooted in Ridge Farm.
Two 2-3 foot diameter trees were blown down and siding was peeled from a building in downtown Ridge Farm.
A hail stone cracked the windshield of a pickup truck.
A large shed was destroyed just east of New Holland, with pieces of it blown across Illinois Route 10.  In addition, most of the roof was torn off an agricultural supply building.
A tree was knocked down in Lincoln.
A tree was blown down across Route 121 and 2000th Avenue.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field southeast of Monticello.  No damage was reported.

A tornado touched down about 3.5 miles northeast of Ivesdale at 4:06 PM CDT then tracked northeastward for 8 miles before lifting 2 miles west of Willard Airport at 4:17 PM CDT.  The tornado damaged the roof and windows of a house, overturned a trailer, damaged a corn crib and chicken coop, and knocked down 6 trees along its path.
A tornado briefly touched down in a field west of Sidney.  No damage was reported.
A tornado touched down just southeast of Tilton at 4:18 PM CDT.  The tornado blew a small carport garage about 75 yards onto a trailer before lifting at 4:19 PM CDT.
The AWOS unit at the Robinson Airport reported a thunderstorm wind gust of 61 mph. No damage was reported.
Numerous tree limbs were blown down in Princeville.
A 4-inch diameter tree limb was blown down at Old Galena Road and Cedar Hills Road southwest of Rome.
Power lines were blown down at 1950 North and 1400 East about 2 miles east of Low Point.

A tornado touched down about 3.2 miles west-southwest of Hoopeston at 5:18 PM CDT.  The tornado tracked eastward, destroying a grain silo, throwing a grain auger into a 20 X 40 shed, and ripping shingles off two houses before lifting 1.1 miles southwest of Hoopeston at 5:23 PM CDT.
Power lines were blown down in Toluca.
A tree was blown down across Winter Avenue a quarter of a mile east of Bowman Avenue.
Power poles were blown down near the junction of highways 1 and 9 near Hoopeston.
Power lines were blown down in Rantoul.  In addition, an SUV window was broken.
Strong thunderstorm winds derailed approximately 30 train cars about 1.5 miles east of Toluca in Marshall County.
Several trees were blown down. The front of a garage was pulled out, and the roof was torn off an outbuilding.
A tree fell onto a vacant house in Williamsville.
A power pole was blown down and two trees were damaged in Elkhart.
Power lines were blown down west of Sherman.
A few trees were blown down and roofing was torn off a home.

Rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour for nearly two hours produced flash flooding of several rural roads and state highways in central and eastern Marshall County. The greatest impact was on Illinois Route 89 south of Varna, Illinois Route 17 between Lacon and Varna, and County Road 2600 East near Toluca, where the roads were flooded and had to be closed during the overnight hours due to more than a foot of accumulated water.

Nearly 3.00 of rain fell in northeast Vermilion County within 90 minutes during the early evening. Streets and rural roads from Hoopeston to 3 miles west of Hoopeston, and along Illinois Route 9 to the Indiana border were impacted by more than a foot of water.

Rural areas of central Effingham County accumulated nearly 4.00 of rain in two hours during the early evening of May 20th. An isolated, slow moving thunderstorm was responsible for the heavy rainfall. Many rural roads south of I-70 and west of I-57, between Altamont and Watson, were inundated.
A lightning strike set a house on fire on Pauli Road in Dunlap.  The house burned to the ground and was a total loss.
A three-foot diameter tree was blown down just southwest of Toulon.

A downburst from an isolated thunderstorm did considerable damage to a school on the south side of Rantoul.  Part of the roof was torn off the Broadmeadow Intermediate Grade Level Center.  Several trees in the immediate area were also blown over.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down.
A tree and several tree limbs were blown down in Washington.
A large tree limb was blown down onto power lines, causing a power outage.
A tree was blown onto a house in Tremont.  Several power lines were knocked down around town as well.
Several power lines were blown down.

A 64 year-old Chillicothe man died as a result of heat stroke on July 5th.  The high temperature at the Peoria Airport reached 101 degrees that day, while heat index values ranged from 105 to 110 degrees.

Rainfall only occurred on 4 days during the month in much of Cass County. At Virginia, only 0.93 of rain was measured, which was more than 3.30 below normal. This was the 6th driest June on record in Virginia. As a result, the county was classified in a severe drought on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Clay County in June. Near Clay City only 0.27 of rain was recorded, which was the driest June on record. At Flora, only 0.84 of rain was measured, which was the 3rd driest June on record. As a result, the county was designated in a Severe Drought on June 22nd. The flow on the Little Wabash River fell below the 10th percentile.  Local officials instituted a ban on open burning.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Crawford County in June. Observers near Palestine and Robinson recorded their driest June on record, with rainfall at Hutsonville coming in as the 2nd driest June on record. As a result, Crawford County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th. Local officials instituted a ban on open burning.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across DeWitt County in June. Observers from Clinton to Farmer City reported only 0.50 to 1.50 of rain for the month. Farmer City had their 5th driest June on record. As a result, DeWitt County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th. Local officials instituted a ban on open burning.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Jasper County in June. The flow of the Embarras River at Ste. Marie was only in the 8th percentile during the last half of the month. As a result, Jasper County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th. Local officials instituted a ban on open burning.

Very warm and dry conditions developed in Lawrence County during June. Rain only occurred twice during the month at Lawrenceville, for a total of 0.09. This was the driest June on record. The flow of the Embarras River at Lawrenceville was only in the 10th percentile. The county was designated in a Severe Drought on June 19th, and an Extreme Drought on June 27th. Local officials instituted a ban on open burning.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Logan County in June. Rainfall in Lincoln only totaled 0.58 for the month, which was the 3rd driest June on record. As a result, Logan County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Macon County in June. Rainfall in Decatur only totaled 0.87 for the month, which was the 7th driest June on record. The water level at Lake Decatur dropped more than a foot during June. The flow on the Sangamon River at Decatur was only in the 1st percentile, and the lowest since 1989. As a result, Macon County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Mason County in June. Rainfall in Havana totaled 2.87, which was 1.88 below normal.  The yearly rainfall deficit since January 1st reached 9.17.  As a result, Mason County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across McLean County in June. Rainfall in Normal totaled 1.88, which was 2.44 below normal.  The yearly rainfall deficit since January 1st reached 9.06.  The flow along Little Kickapoo Creek near Heyworth was the 8th lowest on record.  As a result, McLean County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Richland County in June. Rainfall in Olney totaled just 0.54, making it the second driest June on record.  As a result, Richland County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Tazewell County in June. While monthly rainfall was only about 1 inch below normal, yearly deficits since January 1st were between 6 and 8 inches.  The flow along the Mackinaw River at Green Valley dropped into the 11th percentile.  As a result, Tazewell County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Woodford County in June.  While monthly rainfall was only about 1 inch below normal, yearly deficits since January 1st were between 6 and 8 inches.  The flow along the Mackinaw River at Congerville dropped into the 6th percentile.  As a result, Woodford County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Menard County in June. Rainfall near Petersburg totaled just 0.73, which was 3.14 below normal.  The flow along the Sangamon River at Petersburg was the 5th lowest on record.  As a result, Menard County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.

Very warm and dry conditions developed across Piatt County in June. The flow along the Sangamon River at Monticello dropped to the 2nd percentile. As a result, Piatt County was designated as a Severe Drought area on June 19th.
Several small trees and tree branches were blown down.
Several tree branches were blown down.
A 3-foot diameter tree was blown down across 1600E about 1.5 miles south of 1800N.
Numerous tree branches were blown down between Birds and Russellville.
A tree was blown down 2 miles northwest of St. Francisville.
Tree limbs were blown down onto power lines on Billett Road south of Lawrenceville.
Power lines were blown down onto East 600th Avenue about 3 miles south of Newton.
A tree was blown down at the IL33/49 junction about 6 miles E/NE of Newton.
Trees were blown down...knocking out power in Chauncey.
A large tree was blown down near the intersection of 1750E and 2000N.
Several trees and large tree limbs were blown down.  A small shed was destroyed, and the roof was blown off a pole barn.
The roof of a trailer was damaged, two power poles were snapped, and numerous trees were blown down.
Numerous trees and tree branches were blown down.  Power lines were knocked downed as well, creating a power outage in Armington.  In addition, the roof of an old school was damaged.
A two to three-foot diameter hollow tree branch was broken out of a tree and fell onto a house.  Several other tree branches and power lines were blown down around town.

A wildfire burned 350 acres of grassland near Rochester in Sangamon County on July 27th. While the exact cause of the fire is unknown, it was likely aided by very dry conditions and northwesterly winds gusting to 25 mph. No injuries were reported: however, a barn was destroyed by the fire, a small shed was damaged and several pieces of fire fighting equipment were severly damaged or destroyed.

The hot and dry conditions continued through July in Cass County.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first and third weeks of the month.  Only 0.44 of rain was recorded at Virginia and 0.28 at Beardstown, making it the driest July on record at both locations.  Due to the drought, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Cass County was upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.61 of rain fell in Urbana, making it the 5th driest July on record.  The flow along Boneyard Creek in Urbana dropped to the 12th lowest on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Champaign County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.52 of rain fell in Morrisonville, making it the driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first and third weeks of the month.  As a result of the continued hot and dry conditions, voluntary water restrictions were put into place in Taylorville.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Christian County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.54 of rain fell in Casey, making it the 2nd driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month. Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials. Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Clark County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

The hot and dry conditions continued into July across Clay County.  Only 0.93 of rain was measured at Flora, resulting in the 7th driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred the first 10 days of the month, and the third week of the month.  Streamflow on the Little Wabash River fell below the 10th percentile.  A ban on open burning remained in effect, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Clay County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.08 of rain fell in Charleston, making it the driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  In addition, voluntary water restrictions were put into place for Mattoon.  The flow along the Kaskaskia River at Cooks Mills dropped to the lowest on record.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Coles County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions continued into July across Crawford County.  Extreme heat occurred during the first 10 days of the month, and during the 3rd week, when temperatures rose to 100 degrees or higher.  Robinson recorded their hottest July on record, and Palestine had their 2nd hottest July on record.  Only 0.52 of rain was observed at Robinson during the month, making it the driest July on record.  A ban on open burning continued, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Crawford County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th and an Exceptional Drought on July 31st.

Very hot and dry conditions developed across Cumberland County during the month of July.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Cumberland County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions continued into July across DeWitt County.  Extreme heat occurred during the first week of the month, and during the 3rd week, when temperatures rose to 100 degrees or higher.  The county averaged about 1.00 of rain during the month.  The level of Clinton Lake dropped about one foot during July.   A ban on open burning continued, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  DeWitt County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 1.30 of rain fell in Tuscola, making it the 13th driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  The flow along the Embarras River at Camargo dropped to the lowest on record.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Douglas County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.02 of rain fell in Paris, making it the 2nd driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Edgar County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Very hot and dry conditions developed across Effingham County during the month of July.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Effingham County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.18 of rain fell near Avon, making it the driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  The flow along the Spoon River at Seville dropped into the 13th percentile.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Fulton County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 17th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions continued into July across Jasper County.  Extreme heat occurred during the first 10 days of the month, and during the 3rd week, when temperatures rose to 100 degrees or higher.  The flow along the Embarras River at Ste. Marie remained around the 10th percentile.  A ban on open burning continued, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Jasper County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.85 of rain fell in Galesburg, making it the 3rd driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Knox County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 17th.

Very hot and dry conditions continued into July across Lawrence County.  Temperatures reached at least 100 degrees 11 times during the month.  Only 0.92 of rain was measured in Lawrenceville, which was the 3rd driest July on record.  The flow on the Embarras River at Lawrenceville dropped into the 5th percentile, which was the lowest flow on record.  Burn bans remained in place, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  The county was upgraded to an Exceptional Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions continued into July across Logan County. Extreme heat occurred during the first week of the month, and during the 3rd week, when temperatures rose to 100 degrees or higher five times.  The month was the 10th warmest July on record at Lincoln.  Rainfall at Lincoln was only 1.37.  The flow along the Lake Fork near Cornland was the 10th lowest in the past 65 years, and the lowest since the drought of 1988.  As a result, mandatory water restrictions were established in Latham, voluntary water restrictions were put into place and the bulk water sale station was closed in Mt. Pulaski.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  The county was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions continued into July across Macon County.  Extreme heat occurred during the first week of the month, and during the 3rd week, when temperatures rose to 100 degrees or higher seven times.  The month was the 2nd warmest July on record at Decatur.  Rainfall at Decatur was only 0.47.  The flow along the Sangamon River near Decatur was the 8th lowest in the past 30 years, and the lowest since 1989.  The level at Lake Decatur fell nearly two feet during July.  As a result, mandatory water restrictions were put into place for Decatur and Mt. Zion.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  The county was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 2.00 of rain fell in Lacon, making it the 10th driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  The flow along the Illinois River at Henry dropped to the 8th lowest on record.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Marshall County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 17th.

Only 0.20 of rain fell in Havana, making it the driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Mason County was upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 1.46 of rain fell in Normal, which was 2.49 below normal for the month of July.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  The flow along the Little Kickapoo Creek near Heyworth dropped to the 5th lowest on record.   Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  McLean County was upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.93 of rain fell near Petersburg, making it the 3rd driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  The flow along the Sangamon River at Petersburg was the 3rd lowest on record.   Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Menard County was upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.50 of rain fell near Jacksonville, making it the 2nd driest July on record.  Mandatory water restrictions were established in Jacksonville as a result. Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month. As a result of the hot and dry conditions, local officials instituted a ban on open burning. Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Morgan County was designated  as a Severe Drought area on July 10th, and upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 1.30 of rain fell in Sullivan and Lovington, making it the 2nd driest July on record in Moultrie County.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.   Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Moultrie County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Severe Drought by mid-July. Extreme heat the first week of the month, with 7 days at or above 100 at Peoria for the month. Peoria had the third warmest July on record. Only 1.35 of rainfall at Peoria. Dredging was necessary on the Illinois River south of the Peoria Lock & Dam to keep the channel clear for barge traffic, due to low river levels.

Hot and dry conditions continued in Piatt County during the month of July. Average rainfall in the county for the month was only around 1.00. Extreme heat occurred the first week of the month, with temperatures at or above 100 degrees.  The Sangamon River at Monticello was at zero flow for much of July, which was the lowest flow ever recorded at that site in 105 years.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans due to the hot and dry conditions. Piatt County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Very hot and dry conditions continued into July across Richland County.  Temperatures reached at least 100 degrees 13 times during the month.  Only 1.62 of rain was measured near Olney. Burn bans remained in place, while crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  The county was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Extreme heat the first week of the month with 4 days above 100. A total of 9 days at or above 100 in July. Only 0.34 of rain for the month. Fourth warmest July and third driest July on record in Springfield. Numerous grassland wildfires were reported the last week of the month, prompting burn bans in the county. Flow on the Sangamon River at Riverton was in the 10th to 20th percentile. Lake Springfield levels fell 1.63 ft during the month, prompting water conservation measures for the city of Springfield. Mandatory water restrictions were also established in Williamsville and Sherman.

Only 0.94 of rain fell in Rushville, making it the 11th driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred  five times during the month.   Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Schuyler County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.99 of rain fell in Winchester, making it the 3rd driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred  nine times during the month.   Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Scott County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.19 of rain fell in Windsor and 0.42 was reported in Shelbyville, making it the driest July on record for Shelby County.  Voluntary water restrictions were established in Shelbyville as a result. Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred  eight times during the month.  The heat and dryness caused the level of Lake Shelbyville to fall 0.6 of a foot during July. Due to the extremely dry and hot conditions, a ban on opening burning was instituted by local officials. Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Shelby County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 3rd, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Hot and dry conditions prevailed much of July in Stark County. Between mid-June and mid-July, only 0.50 of rain was reported near Bradford.  Temperatures reached 100 degrees or hotter four times during the month. As a result, a Severe Drought was designated for Stark County on July 17th.

Only 1.00 to 1.25 of rain fell across Tazewell County during the month, which was the 9th driest July on record.  The flow on the Mackinaw River at Green Valley improved slightly from June, but was only around the 20th percentile. Voluntary water restrictions in Groveland,and a countywide burn ban continued as a result. Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred  seven times during the month.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Tazewell County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.

Only 0.26 of rain fell in Danville, making it the driest July on record.  Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred during the first week of the month.  Due to the hot and dry conditions, a ban on open burning was instituted by local officials.  The flow along the Middle Fork of the Vermilion River near Oakwood dropped to the lowest on record.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Vermilion County was classified in a Severe Drought on July 10th, then upgraded to Extreme Drought on July 24th.

An average of only 0.40 of rain fell across Woodford County during the month, which was among the top three driest Julys on record.  The flow on the Mackinaw River at Congerville was only in the 3rd percentile. Voluntary water restrictions were established in El Paso. Extreme heat in excess of 100 degrees occurred  nine times during the month.  Crop stress was extreme for corn and soybeans.  Woodford County was upgraded to an Extreme Drought on July 24th.
A three-foot diameter tree was blown down in Toulon.
Lightning struck Highway 50 in Flora, creating a hole 12 inches wide and 6 inches deep.
A large tree was blown down onto a deck.
Several trees and tree limbs were blown down.  Power lines were also knocked down.
A 13-inch diameter tree was blown down on the 700 block of West 12th Street.
The roof of a building was blown off at the corner of 5th and Walnut Street in Clay City.  The roof of a trailer was also blown off, and a tree was knocked down onto a house.
Numerous trees and tree branches were blown down in Danvers.

Downburst winds of 70 to 80 mph produced a wide swath of damage from Danvers southeastward into the southwest side of Bloomington.  One of the hardest hit locations along this path was the Apollo Acres subdivision just north of Illinois Route 9, where 159 homes sustained damage.  139 of those homes had awnings or shingles damaged, while 19 suffered minor roof and window damage, and 1 home had one-third of its roof torn off.  Total damage in Apollo Acres was around $1 million.  Other significant damage occurred along the path of the storm, including numerous downed trees, trailers blown over, and several large metal buildings with doors blown in and roofs torn off.  Total damage to 30 businesses along the path was estimated at around $2.5 million.  One minor injury was reported, as a car was hit by a wind-blown trailer.
Hail damaged crops along a 1.5 mile-long/50 yards-wide swath just north of Heyworth.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Toluca.
A 12-inch diameter tree was blown down, bringing a power line down with it.  A road was blocked by the tree.
Ten train cars were derailed by strong winds about 3 miles south of Sidney.
Several tree limbs were blown down.
Numerous tree branches were blown down.
A few trees were topped and several power lines were blown down just south of Sidney.  In addition, a corn field was flattened.

Numerous trees and tree branches were blown down.  Roof damage was reported to 29 structures.  A garage was destroyed and several machine sheds were severely damaged or destroyed.  In addition, a grain silo was damaged.
Three power poles were snapped and several tree branches were blown down.
Three large trees were blown down.
A tree branch was blown onto a vehicle on County Road 1100 North about 1.5 miles north of Sidney.

Strong thunderstorm winds produced damage across a 2 square mile area on the west and southwest side of Champaign.  Numerous tree branches and power lines were blown down, creating a power outage for several hours.  The damage was bounded by Springfield Avenue on the north, Prospect Avenue on the east, Windsor Avenue on the south, and Duncan Road on the west.
Several 5 to 6-inch diameter tree branches were blown down at the high school.
Numerous 12 to 18-inch diameter trees were blown down.  Power lines were knocked down as well.
Two power poles were snapped along 4th Street in Pawnee.
A 2-foot diameter tree was blown down.  Numerous tree branches were knocked down as well, many of which blocked roads.
Several power poles and power lines were blown down.  The siding was torn off a trailer.
A 3-foot diameter tree was uprooted.
Numerous trees and power poles were blown down across Mattoon.  Electricity was knocked out to many residents for about 2 hours.  Power lines were blown down and blocked Lake Mattoon Road.
Several trees were blown down about 1 mile east of Gays.

Numerous trees were blown down and a few power poles were snapped along Route 16 west of Mattoon.  Two people were injured when they were hit by falling tree branches as they were trying to take shelter from the storm.  A semi and trailer were blown over on Route 16 2 miles west of Mattoon.  Many corn fields sustained wind damage as well.
A tree was blown down about 1 mile northwest of Oskaloosa near the Clay and Marion County line.
Numerous trees were blown down, including a 20-inch diameter tree that fell onto power lines.  Power was knocked out throughout Martinsville.
Several trees were blown down in Robinson.

Hundreds of trees were uprooted in the town of Windsor. Several trees and large branches damaged about 200 house roofs in town. The strong wind also blew shingles off of many houses. One house on the west side of town was pushed several inches off of its foundation. Power poles snapped, power lines were knocked down and a few flag poles were bent.
A gabled roof of a church was torn off.  Numerous trees and tree branches were blown down across town.
Several tree limbs were blown down across Charleston.  A power pole was knocked down as well.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in Lerna.

Numerous trees and tree branches were blown down across Cumberland County.  Large branches were knocked down onto 3 houses in Janesville.  Power lines were blown down, resulting in a power outage in Greenup.
Several trees were blown down in various locations across Effingham County.
A tree was blown down about 1 mile west of Louisville.
A tree was blown down in Flora, and another was knocked down about 1 mile northwest of town.

More than 30 homes and businesses along the Illinois River in Marshall County suffered damage due to record river levels. The river stage at Henry climbed to a record level of 32.87 feet on April 22nd at 16:00 local time, which was nearly 10 feet above flood stage. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

Numerous homes along the Illinois river in Chillicothe, Rome, Mossville and Mapleton suffered damage due to record river levels. Several businesses along the Illinois River in downtown Peoria were also damaged by the flooding. The river stage at Peoria climbed to a record level of 29.35 feet on April 23rd at 19:30 local time, which was nearly 12 feet above flood stage. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

Around 276 homes, two businesses, a fire station and numerous roads along the Illinois river in Spring Bay and Bay View Gardens were inundated, and suffered damage due to record river levels. The river stage at Peoria climbed to a record level of 29.35 feet on April 23rd at 19:30 local time, which was nearly 12 feet above flood stage. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

Several homes and businesses along the Illinois river in Tazewell suffered damage due to record river levels. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

No homes were damaged by record levels of flooding on the Illinois River. However, thousands of acres of agricultural land and nature reserves were inundated by the flood waters. Several roads along the river were also damaged. The river stage at Havana climbed to a record level of 27.78 feet on April 25th at 19:15 local time, which was nearly 14 feet above flood stage. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

Hundreds of cabins and sheds in wildlife areas along the Illinois River were severely damaged. In addition, 25 homes and several other structures were damaged near Bath, Snicarte, Havana and Goofy Ridge. Nearly 15 miles of roads will need to be rebuilt due to the flooding. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

Several structures southwest of Beardstown in rural parts of Cass County were damaged by record levels of flooding on the Illinois River. A few structures in rural parts of extreme northwest Morgan County were damaged by near record levels of flooding on the Illinois River. The river stage at Meredosia climbed to a level of 28.60 feet on April 27th, which was only one-tenth of a foot lower than the all time record. This crest was nearly 12 feet above flood stage. High impact flooding continued into the month of May 2013.

A tornado touched down in far eastern Peoria County about 4 miles ENE of Mapleton at 10:52 AM CST.  The tornado uprooted dozens of trees and snapped several power poles before crossing the Illinois River into Tazewell County at 10:53 AM CST.

This tornado crossed the Illinois River from Peoria County at 10:53 AM CST.  It tracked through the northwest side of Pekin before lifting 2 miles northeast of Pekin at 10:54 AM CST.  Approximately 179 houses and 6 businesses suffered major damage, while 182 houses experienced minor roof damage.  In addition, 3 apartment buildings lost their roofs, a power substation had minor damage, and hundreds of cars were damaged.  Ten people were injured.

A tornado touched down 2.4 miles SE of East Peoria at 10:59 AM CST, then tracked northeastward through parts of East Peoria and Washington before crossing the border into Woodford County at 11:12 AM CST.  One man in Washington was killed by the tornado, one woman from Washington died 11 days later from multiple serious injuries sustained by the tornado, one man died six weeks later from injuries sustained by the tornado, and 121 people were injured.|  |In East Peoria: 20 homes were destroyed, while 75 homes, 7 businesses, and 5 apartment buildings suffered major damage.  Minor damage occurred to 137 homes and 3 businesses.  In addition, nearly 400 vehicles were damaged, thousands of trees and numerous power poles were destroyed.  The estimated damage in East Peoria stands at $110 million.||In Washington: The tornado increased to EF4 intensity and widened to between 1/4 and 1/2 mile wide.  633 homes, 7 businesses, 7 apartment buildings, and 2,500 vehicles were destroyed.  Major damage occurred to 280 homes, 2 businesses, the roof of a school, and several outbuildings.  Minor damage occurred to another 190 homes.  Thousands of trees and power poles were snapped.  Nearly 5,000 people were in the path of this tornado: however, injury and fatality totals were relatively low due to early warning and the fact that many people were either in church or out of town at the time. The tornado moved out of the Washington city limits and across another 2 miles of rural Tazewell County before crossing the border into Woodford County.  Total damage in Washington is estimated at $800 million.

This tornado crossed the border from Tazewell County at 11:12 AM CST, then tracked northeastward across rural Woodford County before entering into far southern LaSalle County in National Weather Service Chicago's County Warning Area (CWA) at 11:33 AM CST.  It weakened a bit to EF3 intensity but remained between 1/4 and 1/2 mile wide as it crossed into Woodford County.  During much of its time in Woodford County, the tornado traveled across open fields, impacting dozens of farmsteads.  Nearly 70 farm buildings and 7 homes were destroyed.  Major damage occurred to 17 homes, while 23 others received minor damage.  About 100 vehicles were damaged, including several semi trucks at a truck stop north of Minonk.  Three people were injured in overturned semi trucks.  One cell tower was toppled and hundreds of power poles and trees were snapped.  Total damage from the tornado was estimated at $25 million.

A tornado touched down on the north side of Pana at 12:15 PM CST, then tracked northeastward before lifting 3.1 miles NNE of Pana at 12:18 PM CST.  Several homes suffered roof damage near the intersection of Almond and Elm streets on the north side of Pana.  Trees were blown down, damaging 3 cars.  Numerous power lines were knocked down as well.  The tornado moved NNE, damaging a house and destroying an outbuilding before dissipating in an open field.

A tornado touched down on the northwest side of West Liberty at 12:25 PM CST, then tracked northeastward before lifting 3.4 miles ENE of West Liberty at 12:29 PM CST.  Roof and siding damage occurred to 12 homes, while the roof was completely torn off an older one-story house.  A semi-truck was overturned and several trees were uprooted.  A barn was destroyed and 2 sheds had their roofs torn off about 1 mile ENE of West Liberty before the tornado dissipated.

This tornado continued from Fayette County in National Weather Service St. Louis' County Warning Area (CWA).  The tornado crossed into Effingham County 3.2 miles WNW of Altamont at 12:28 PM CST before tracking northeastward and dissipating 2.9 miles NNW of Altamont at 12:32 PM CST.  About a dozen outbuildings were damaged and minor damage occurred to the roofs of 3 homes.  Several power poles were blown down as well.  The tornado dissipated near North 200th Street and East 1300th Avenue in rural Effingham County.

A tornado touched down in an open field about 3 miles NE of Lovington at 12:30 PM CST, then tracked northeastward and crossed into Douglas County about 5 miles north of Arthur at 12:37 PM CST.  Major roof damage occurred to 8 homes, while 1 garage was destroyed and 17 outbuildings were severely damaged.  Numerous trees and power poles were snapped.

This tornado crossed into Douglas County from Moultrie County about 5 miles north of Arthur at 12:37 PM CST, then tracked northeastward before lifting 0.8 miles east of Garrett at 12:41 PM CST.  The tornado damaged the roofs of 3 homes and 5 outbuildings, as well as, numerous trees and power poles in rural western Douglas County.  It then crossed U.S. Highway 36 and tracked into the town of Garrett where it damaged the roofs of about two dozen homes and mobile homes before dissipating.

A tornado touched down 3.7 miles NW of Tuscola at 12:44 PM CST, then tracked northeastward and crossed into Champaign County about 1.5 miles NW of Villa Grove at 12:52 PM CST.  The roof of a house and 2 outbuildings were damaged during the first 2 miles of the track.  The tornado strengthened after it crossed U.S. Highway 45 doing major damage to 2 homes, several large farm buildings, numerous power poles, and a garage.  The tornado then turned to the east, damaging the roofs of two homes and destroying several outbuildings.  It then crossed I-57 near mile marker 218 where it destroyed a mobile home just east of the highway.  The tornado did major damage to several more roofs and outbuildings before it merged with another tornado 2 miles WNW of Villa Grove, turned to the northeast, and crossed into Champaign County.

This tornado crossed from Douglas County into Champaign County 5.3 miles SE of Pesotum at 12:52 PM CST, then tracked northeastward before lifting 2.7 NNW of Broadlands at 1:02 PM CST.  The tornado moved through open fields for the first 2.5 miles in Champaign County, then took the roof off 1 home, destroyed about a dozen outbuildings, snapped numerous power poles and trees, and did roof damage to 6 homes.  The tornado dissipated in a field 2.7 NNW of Broadlands.

A tornado touched down in an open field about 1 mile SE of Thomasboro at 12:45 PM CST and rapidly moved to the northeast.  In less than a minute it increased in intensity, causing damage to 3 nearby farms and pushing 2 farm houses off their foundations.  The tornado moved through open fields for about 2 miles at which time it widened to nearly 1/4 mile wide and became wrapped in rain.  It destroyed 3 homes, several outbuildings, and damaged a few other homes before it moved into the town of Gifford.  The rain-wrapped tornado was about 1/2 mile wide when it moved through the center of Gifford.  Nearly 30 homes were destroyed, more than 40 suffered major damage, and around 125 had minor damage.  Around 15 businesses sustained moderate to major damage and the roof of a school was peeled back.  Hundreds of vehicles were damaged or destroyed.  The tornado tracked for another 5 miles to the northeast, destroying 3 homes and numerous outbuildings, damaging several other homes, and snapping many trees and power poles.  The tornado crossed into Vermilion County about 3 miles NNE of Penfield at 1:00 PM CST.  Six people were injured and total damage was estimated at $60 million.

This tornado crossed from Champaign County into Vermilion County 4.1 miles NW of Armstrong at 1:00 PM CST, then tracked northeastward across rural northwest Vermilion County.  The tornado destroyed 1 home, 20 outbuildings, and a camper.  It also damaged 7 other homes and snapped numerous power poles and trees.  The tornado weakened as it moved out of Vermilion County into Iroquois County in National Weather Service Chicago's County Warning Area (CWA) about 3.7 miles WNW of Hoopeston at 1:14PM CST.

A tornado touched down in a field just west of mile marker 216 along I-57 at 12:46 PM CST, then tracked northeastward before dissipating 2 miles WNW of Villa Grove at 12:51 PM CST.  The tornado crossed the interstate, then destroyed 3 outbuildings and damaged the roofs of 2 homes.  For the next 4 miles, it moved through mainly open fields, damaging trees and power lines.  The tornado dissipated about 2 miles WNW of Villa Grove when it merged with a larger tornado that was moving ENE across north-central Douglas County.

A tornado touched down in an open field 2.8 miles NE of Allerton at 1:03 PM CST.  The tornado tracked to the northeast for about 15 miles and did major damage to 2 homes, roof damage to 4 other homes, and destroyed 9 outbuildings, 4 garages, and 2 grain bins.  Numerous trees and power poles were also snapped.  The tornado crossed State Route 1 about 2 miles north of Westville, impacting the villages of Belgium and Hegeler where 1 person was injured.  Nine homes sustained major damage, 26 had significant roof damage, and more than 100 had minor roof damage.  The tornado also damaged more than 50 mobile homes, numerous garages and vehicles, and destroyed about 25 outbuildings.  The tornado crossed the Vermilion River and moved through about a mile of forested area before dissipating 4.4 miles NE of Westville and 3 miles W of the Indiana border.  Total damage was estimated at $9.5 million.

A snowplow driver was killed when he got out of his vehicle to assist a stranded motorist.  A vehicle traveling down Route 17 about 3 miles from Toulon lost control on the slippery, snow-covered road and hit the snowplow driver.  He was later pronounced dead at a local hospital.
A tornado briefly touched down in an open field about 0.7 miles north of Bethel.  No damage was reported.
A tornado briefly touched down about 1.7 miles east of Divernon at 3:43 PM CST.  The tornado tore the roof off a barn before lifting at 3:44 PM CST.

A tornado touched down at 3:57 PM CST 3 miles south of Mechanicsburg.  The tornado tracked northeastward damaging numerous outbuildings and the roofs of several homes.  A trailer was flipped over, multiple power poles were snapped, and numerous trees were damaged as well before the tornado lifted 2.6 miles west of Illiopolis at 4:06 PM CST.

This tornado crossed from Montgomery County in the National Weather Service St. Louis County Warning Area (CWA) into Shelby County about 2.6 miles northwest of Oconee at 4:14 PM CST.  Mainly tree damage occurred along the path of the tornado before it crossed into Christian County 4.4 miles north-northeast of Oconee at 4:19 PM CST.

This tornado crossed into Christian County from Shelby County 2.9 miles south of Pana at 4:19 PM CST.  The tornado damaged several outbuildings, trees and a garage south and east of Pana before crossing back into Shelby County 3.0 miles east of Pana at 4:25 PM CST.

This tornado crossed into Shelby County from Christian County 3.6 miles west of Tower Hill at 4:25 PM CST.  The tornado increased in intensity, doing significant damage to the roof of a house and causing one minor injury about 3 miles north-northwest of Tower Hill.  The tornado continued to the northeast, dissipating near the intersection of county roads 1700 North and 1200 East, or 3 miles west-southwest of Westerveldt at 4:33 PM CST.
A tornado briefly touched down in an open field 3.3 miles west-southwest of Findlay at 4:40 PM CST.  The tornado dissipated at 4:41 PM CST with no damage reported.

A tornado touched down in an open field 4 miles west-southwest of Shumway at 4:54 PM CST.  The tornado tracked northeastward, crossing state highway 33 between Shumway and Beecher City.  The tornado snapped several power poles as it crossed the highway before dissipating in an open field 3 miles west-northwest of Shumway at 4:56 PM CST.

A tornado touched down 3.9 miles west-southwest of Chrisman.  It crossed U.S. Highway 36 near 1275th St. and tracked another 1.5 miles, dissipating before it reached 1400th St.  No damage was reported.

A tornado touched down in an open field 2.4 miles west of Concord at 2:52 PM CST.  The tornado tracked northeastward and crossed into Cass County 5.5 miles northeast of Concord at 2:59 PM CST.  No damage was reported.
This tornado crossed into Cass County from Morgan County 3.8 miles east of Arenzville at 2:59 PM CST.  It dissipated 4.5 miles east of Arenzville at 3:00 PM CST with no damage reported.

Very heavy rainfall of 2.50 to 3.00 inches between 1800 and 1900 CST resulted in rapid flash flooding in a small part of southeast Woodford County. Illinois Route 251 and County Road 9  west of Kappa were inundated with water 12 to 18 inches deep. Roads were closed for nearly three hours. The water receded quickly and the flooding ended by late evening.

Very heavy rainfall of 2.50 to 3.00 inches between 1800 and 1900 CST resulted in rapid flash flooding in a small part of northwest McLean County. County Road 8 near the north edge of Lake Bloomington and County Road 29 south of Gridley were inundated with water 12 to 18 inches deep. These roads, as well as several rural roads, were closed for nearly three hours. The water receded quickly and the flooding ended by late evening.

Persistent rain from numerous thunderstorms tracking over the same areas produced 3.00 to 4.00 inches in less than two hours during the early evening hours. Numerous roads were impassable in Savoy, Tolono and rural areas of south central Champaign County. U.S. Highway 45 and State Route 130 were also significantly impacted and closed in spots.

Persistent rain from numerous thunderstorms tracking over the same areas produced 3.00 inches in less than two hours during the early evening hours in a small part of east central Piatt County. Persistent rain from numerous thunderstorms tracking over the same areas produced 2.50 to 3.00 inches in less than two hours during the early evening hours in a small portion of northeast Douglas County. Numerous rural roads were impassable and closed as a result.

A second band of persistent rain from numerous thunderstorms tracking over the same areas in Champaign County produced 2.50 to 3.00 inches in less than two hours during the early evening hours east of Urbana. Most streets in St. Joseph and Ogden were flooded. Numerous rural roads in extreme east central Champaign County were impassable. State Highway 49 and Interstate 74 from mile post 191 to 198 were impacted and traffic was stopped at times.

Two bands of persistent rain from numerous thunderstorms tracking over the same areas in central and southern Vermilion County produced 3.00 to 4.00 inches in less than two hours during the evening. State Highway 1 from Georgetown to the Edgar County Line and Interstate 74 from mile post 198 to 203 were impacted and traffic was stopped at times.

Heavy rainfall, with accumulations of 2.50 to 3.50 in one hour resulted in flash flooding in Springfield and adjacent areas. Numerous streets and viaducts were closed due to the flooding, several vehicles were stranded and water rescues were made by first responders.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.00 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding around the city of Decatur as well as rural areas toward Piatt and Moultrie County. A large part of Main Street in Decatur was closed for two hours due to the flooding. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural Macon County. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.00 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding of rural areas in southwest Piatt County. Streets in Cerro Gordo were flooded, as were parts of Illinois Route 32 and 105. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural Piatt County. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.00 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding of rural areas in northern Moultrie County. Streets in Lovington and Lake City were flooded, as were parts of Illinois Route 32 and 133. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural Moultrie County. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 1.50 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding in northern Clark County. Streets in Marshall were flooded, as were parts of Illinois Route 1 and U.S. Highway 40. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural Clark County, especially along and south of I-70. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.00 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding of mainly rural areas in northeast Coles County. Streets in Oakland were flooded. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural northeast Coles County between Oakland and Ashmore. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.00 to 3.00 in one hour resulted in flash flooding of mainly rural areas in extreme western Edgar County. Numerous rural roads were impassable and standing water was reported around the intersection of Illinois Routes 33 and 49. The flooding subsided rapidly before daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.50 to 4.00 in two hours resulted in flash flooding of northern Scott County. Streets in the town of Bluffs were flooded, as was Illinois Route 100 from just north of I-72 through Bluffs. In addition, standing water was reported on I-72 near the Scott - Pike County line. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural northern Scott County. The flooding subsided rapidly around daybreak.

Heavy rain accumulation of 2.50 to 4.00 in two hours resulted in flash flooding of northwest Morgan County. Numerous rural roads were impassable in rural northwest Morgan County, as were parts of U.S. Highway 67 and Illinois Route 100 northwest of the town of Bethel. The flooding subsided rapidly around daybreak.

Heavy rainfall amounts of 2.50 to 5.10 inches fell on the Springfield Metro area in less than two hours during the evening of August 28th. Multiple viaducts were flooded in Springfield, streets were inundated with water at least 2 feet deep, vehicles were stranded and parts of Interstates 72 and 55 were closed. Nearly 250 water rescues were performed by the Springfield Fire Department for stranded motorists. No injuries were reported.

Heavy rainfall amounts of 2.50 to 5.10 inches fell on the Springfield Metro area in less than two hours during the evening of August 28th. Multiple viaducts were flooded in Springfield, streets were inundated with water at least 2 feet deep, vehicles were stranded and parts of Interstates 72 and 55 were closed. Nearly 250 water rescues were performed by the Springfield Fire Department for stranded motorists. No injuries were reported. The rainfall ended prior to 10:30 pm LST, but the flooding in the city of Springfield lingered until 4:30 am LST due to the amount of rainfall and an overload of water on the city sewer system.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 4.00 inches of rain in less than two hours across a small part of rural, eastern Sangamon County. Most rural roads were impassable between Illiopolis and Mechanicsburg. Parts of I-72 between mileposts 117 and 120 had standing water and lane closures. The flooding quickly subsided by Midnight local time.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 4.00 inches of rain in less than two hours across a small part of northwest Christian County. Most rural roads were impassable between Edinburg and Mt. Auburn. This was the second time within three days that flash flooding was reported in northwest Christian County. The flooding quickly subsided shortly after Midnight local time.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 4.00 inches of rain in less than two hours across southwest Logan County and western parts of the city of Lincoln. Most rural roads were impassable between New Holland, Lincoln and Middletown. State Route 10 west of Lincoln was closed for a short period of time, and streets in the western half of Lincoln were inundated. The flooding quickly subsided in less than three hours.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 4.00 inches of rain in less than two hours across a small part of rural, northeast Menard County. Most rural roads were impassable between Sweetwater and Middletown. The flooding quickly subsided in less than three hours.

A slow moving thunderstorm in southwest Clay County produced 4.00 to 6.00 of rain in a two period during the late evening of August 20th. Multiple streets in Flora and Xenia were flooded. Nearly all rural roads in southwest Clay County were impassable. Parts of Old Highway 50, west of Flora, were closed for a period of time around Midnight local time.

A severe thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 3.00 of rain within one hour in parts of central DeWitt County, including the city of Clinton. The flash flooding resulted in the closure of numerous streets and viaducts in Clinton, as well as basement flooding to numerous homes and businesses. The flash flooding also impacted several rural roads between Clinton and Weldon Springs State Park. The flooding subsided by late evening.

A severe thunderstorm produced 2.00 to 3.00 of rain within one hour in parts of central Macon County, including the cities of Decatur and Mt. Zion. The flash flooding resulted in the closure of numerous streets and viaducts in Decatur, as well as basement flooding to numerous homes and businesses. The flash flooding also impacted several rural roads from Harristown through Decatur to Mt. Zion. The flooding subsided by late evening.

A severe thunderstorm produced 2.50 to 4.00 of rain within 90 minutes in northwest and central Christian County, including parts of the city of Taylorville. Most rural roads from Taylorville to Edinburg and Kincaid were impassable. Some city streets and basements in homes in northwestern portions of Taylorville were also flooded. Illinois Routes 29 and 104 from Taylorville to Kincaid were closed for a period of time during the late evening. The flooding subsided by Midnight local time.

Heavy downpours which produced 2 to 3 inches of rain per hour between 2200-0000 local time resulted in flash flooding across the southern half of Effingham County. Numerous rural roads were impassable, streets in the towns of Mason and Edgewood were flooded, and parts of U.S. Highway 45 near the Clay County line were closed. Several motorists had to be rescued after they drove into flooded ditches. The flooding subsided within three hours.

Heavy downpours which produced 2 to 3 inches of rain per hour between 2200-0000 local time resulted in flash flooding across the northern half of Clay County. Numerous rural roads were impassable, streets were flooded in the town of Hord, and parts of U.S. Highway 45 from the Effingham County line to about Louisville were closed. The flooding subsided within three hours.

Heavy downpours which produced 2 to 3 inches of rain per hour between 2230-0030 local time resulted in flash flooding across much of Jasper County. Numerous rural roads were impassable, streets were flooded in Newton, and parts of Illinois Route 33 from Newton to the Crawford County line, as well as Illinois Route 130 just south of Newton, were closed. The flooding subsided within three hours.

Heavy downpours which produced 2 to 3 inches of rain per hour between 2300-0100 local time resulted in flash flooding across a large part of Crawford County. Numerous rural roads were impassable, streets were flooded in Robinson and Oblong, and two state highways were closed, including Illinois Route 1 from Robinson to Hutsonville and Illinois Route 33 from the Jasper County line to Palestine. The flooding subsided within three hours.

Persistent thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed over the same areas of western Knox County during the early morning hours of September 4th. Observers reported 3.00 to 5.00 inches of rain in the two hours between 0330 and 0530 local time. Numerous streets within Galesburg and Knoxville were flooded. Multiple viaducts flooded which caused several stalled vehicles to become trapped in the rising water during the morning commute. The flooding subsided before late morning.

Slow moving thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall produced an average of 3.50 of rain in less than two hours across central and eastern Schuyler County. Streets in Rushville were flooded as a result. Nearly all rural roads in the county, north and east-northeast of Rushville were impassable. Illinois Route 100 near Browning and parts of U.S. Highway 24 from Rushville to the Fulton County line were closed. The flooding subsided within about three hours by mid-afternoon.

Slow moving thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall produced an average of 3.00 of rain in less than two hours in extreme southern Fulton County. Rural roads within one to two miles of the Schuyler County line were impassable. U.S. Highway 24 from two miles west-southwest of Astoria to the Schuyler County line was closed. The flooding subsided within about three hours by mid-afternoon.

A second round of very heavy rain in less than 24 hours resulted in renewed flash flooding in much of Schuyler County during the morning hours of September 10th. An additional 3.00 to 4.00 inches of rain was reported in less than three hours. Due to the saturated ground, flash flooding developed quickly. Nearly all rural roads in the county were impassable. Most streets in Rushville flooded, as did Illinois Route 67 from Rushville to Littleton. Parts of Illinois Route 101 near the LaMoine River and the town of Brooklyn were closed. The flooding subsided around midday.

A tornado touched down 3.4 miles east of Moweaqua along county road 1000E between county roads 2800N and 2900N at 3:54 PM CDT.  Two machine sheds were destroyed and several trees were broken at this location.  As the tornado tracked northward, it struck a farmstead along the Shelby/Macon county line just east of county road 1000E.  The house sustained major damage to its roof and windows on the south side of the building, with significant damage to an attached garage.  Several trees were snapped and outbuildings were destroyed before the tornado crossed into southern Macon County at 3:56 PM CDT.

This tornado crossed from Shelby County into southern Macon County 4.6 southeast of Macon at 3:56 PM CDT.  The tornado flattened several areas of corn and soybeans from along Crosson Road northeastward past Walker Road, with the greatest crop damage occurring along East Andrews Street Road between Cornthwaite and Sanner Roads.  The tornado continued northeastward, damaging the roof of a barn before dissipating 2 miles west-southwest of Mt. Zion at 4:07 CDT.

A tornado briefly touched down south of the Decatur Airport along Illinois Route 121 just south of the US-36 intersection at 4:12 PM CDT.  A traffic signal mast was snapped, power lines were knocked down, two trees were snapped, and a shed and dumpster were overturned.  The tornado quickly dissipated by 4:13 PM CDT.

A tornado touched down 3.7 miles northeast of Argenta near Friends Creek County Park at 4:29 PM CDT, then tracked northeastward to near the intersection of Macon, Piatt, and DeWitt counties along Illinois Route 48 near Lake Fork before dissipating at 4:33 PM CDT.  The tornado remained in open fields and caused no damage.

Rainfall rates of more than 1.00 inch per hour for at least two hours during the late afternoon, resulted in flash flooding across parts of western and northern Effingham County. Numerous rural roads were impassable. In addition, recreational roads around Lake Sara were inundated and the lake area was closed to traffic. Total rainfall was around 4.00 inches from just east of Altamont to the town of Shumway during the late afternoon and early evening. The flash flooding subsided by late evening.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall amounts of 2.00 to 3.00 inches in less than two hours during the late afternoon hours across northern and central Vermilion County. Many county roads north of Danville became impassable due to high water.  Two cars became submerged on East 2550 North Road just west of IL Route 1, a few miles southwest of Bismarck. Locations in and near Kickapoo State Park were also inundated due to rapidly rising water and flooded roads. The Vermilion River west of Danville also came out of its banks quickly, resulting in the evacuation of a subdivision. No injuries were reported.
